lessons.title: Car Ownership Basics: Buying vs. Leasing

sections.question: Which step can help you compare vehicles before buying?

options.text: Research purchase options, resale value, and insurance costs
Choose a vehicle without checking how it fits your needs
Exchange money and keys without reviewing documents

sections.explanation: Research can help you compare how a vehicle fits your needs and understand costs beyond its sticker price.

children.text: Before choosing a vehicle, consider its purpose, safety features, fuel or battery efficiency, price, insurance costs, purchase or lease options, and resale value.
Hypothetical example:
Sam needs a car for commuting. Sam compares two suitable vehicles, asks about insurance costs, reviews fuel efficiency and resale value, and test-drives both before deciding.

items.question: Can the type of vehicle affect insurance costs?

children.text: Yes. The sources advise checking insurance costs while researching vehicles.

items.question: What should I check when viewing a used vehicle's registration?

children.text: Check that it shows the owner’s legal ownership and that details such as the make, model, and Vehicle Identification Number match the vehicle.

sources.title: Steps to buying a used vehicle
Buy a new vehicle

sections.question: What must parents choose when sharing EI parental benefits?

options.text: The same option, either standard or extended

sections.explanation: Parents who share EI parental benefits must both use the same option: standard or extended.

children.text: EI parental benefits may be paid to a biological, legal, or adoptive parent. Eligible parents may also share them, but both must select the same option.
Hypothetical example:
Two eligible parents plan time away from work to care for their adopted child. They decide to share parental benefits and both select the standard option.

items.question: Do parental benefits cover adoption?

children.text: Yes. They may support an eligible parent caring for a child placed with them for adoption.

items.question: When can parental benefit payments begin?

children.text: They can begin with the week of birth or the week a child is placed with the claimant for adoption.

sources.title: Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles Chapter 13 - Section 1
Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles Chapter 24 - Section 15

sections.question: Which factor should you consider before choosing an investment?
sections.explanation: Your financial goals, financial situation, investment time horizon, and risk tolerance can help you decide whether an investment meets your needs.

children.text: Investment costs can arise when buying, selling, or managing an investment. Understanding these costs matters because they may reduce your return.
Hypothetical example:
Priya compares two investments that suit her goal and risk tolerance. Before choosing, she reviews each investment’s buying, selling, and management costs.

items.question: Where can I find unbiased investing resources?

children.text: Each province or territory has a securities regulator that offers resources to help people get started.

items.question: Do all investments have the same costs?

children.text: No. Costs vary by investment type and may apply when buying, selling, or managing an investment.

sources.title: Basics of investing

sections.question: Which statement about the Métis is supported by the source?

options.text: They are a distinct people and Nation.
They are Indigenous people only of the Arctic.
They are another name for all First Nations.

sections.explanation: The Métis are a distinct people and Nation. Inuit are Indigenous people of the Arctic, and First Nations have their own identities.

children.text: Language matters. First Nations, Métis, and Inuit are distinct groups, and it is best to ask an Indigenous person which term they prefer.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is speaking with a new colleague. Instead of guessing the colleague’s identity, Sam respectfully asks which term the colleague prefers.

items.question: What does “time immemorial” mean?

children.text: It means before memory or record.

items.question: What can a territory acknowledgment recognize?

children.text: It can honour the Indigenous Peoples and histories present on the land.

sources.title: WelcomeBC - Choose BC- WelcomeBC

sections.question: A message claims to be from a government department and asks you to click a link immediately. What should you do?

options.text: Click the link before it expires
Contact the department directly through its official website
Reply with personal information to confirm your identity

sections.explanation: Urgent demands and unexpected links can be signs of a scam. Contact the department directly instead of using the message's link.

children.text: Caller ID can be faked, so a familiar number does not prove that a caller is legitimate. Verify unexpected requests through an official channel.
Hypothetical example:
Lina receives a call asking for her immigration file number and immediate payment. She shares nothing, ends the call, and checks the request through the official government website.

items.question: Which web addresses can help identify an official Government of Canada website?

children.text: Look for websites that begin with
canada.ca
or end with
.gc.ca

items.question: What should I do with a suspicious link asking for banking passwords?

children.text: Do not click the link or provide information. Check the sender’s identity through a trusted channel.

sources.title: Scams and fraud
Fraud targeting newcomers

sections.question: What should you do if you are unsure whether a government message is genuine?

options.text: Contact the department or agency directly
Pay immediately through the message link

sections.explanation: Contacting the department or agency directly helps you verify the message without relying on its links or contact details.

children.text: Urgent payment demands, threats, and requests for personal or financial information can be warning signs. Caller ID can also be faked, so it does not prove who is contacting you.
Hypothetical example:
Sam receives a call that appears to come from a government agency. The caller demands immediate payment. Sam ends the call and contacts the agency directly using its official website.

items.question: Can a realistic-looking government message still be false?

children.text: Yes. Scammers can use artificial intelligence to create realistic messages, images, and websites.

items.question: Does a familiar number on caller ID prove a caller is genuine?

children.text: No. Scammers can use technology to make a phone number appear real.

sources.title: Scams and fraud
Fraud targeting newcomers

sections.question: What should you do if a message claiming to be from a government agency seems suspicious?

options.text: Contact the agency directly using its official website
Click the message link to check whether it is real
Reply with personal information to confirm your identity

sections.explanation: Contact the agency directly. Do not use the message link or provide personal information.

children.text: Urgent payment demands, threats, and requests for personal information can be signs of a scam. Caller ID can also be faked, so verify the sender through an official channel.
Hypothetical example:
Lina receives a threatening call about her immigration status. She shares no information and checks the claim through the official government website instead of trusting the displayed phone number.

items.question: Can a familiar number on caller ID prove that a call is genuine?

children.text: No. Scammers can use technology to make a phone number appear real.

items.question: Should I report a scam if I did not lose money?

children.text: Yes. The Government of Canada says to report all scams or fraud to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, even if you were not a victim.

sources.title: Scams and fraud - Government of Canada
Fraud targeting newcomers

sections.question: Which cost should a buyer consider in addition to the home's purchase price?

options.text: Utilities, insurance, taxes and other fees

sections.explanation: The total cost of owning a home can include utilities, homeowners insurance, taxes and other fees.

children.text: Incentives may reduce some buying costs, but affordability also depends on ongoing housing expenses and the costs in the chosen community.
Hypothetical example:
A buyer compares two homes and reviews utilities, insurance, taxes, other fees and access to needed services before deciding which one fits their finances.

items.question: Do homeownership costs vary by location?

children.text: Yes. Costs vary widely among provinces, territories, cities and neighbourhoods.

items.question: What should I consider before choosing a community?

children.text: Consider affordability, nearby services and amenities, and your short-term and long-term housing needs.

sources.title: Newcomers: An overview of housing in Canada

sections.question: Which home type shares a wall with another house?

options.text: Condominium unit because it always has private exterior walls

sections.explanation: A townhouse shares a wall with another house. A detached house stands on its own, while condominium buildings contain separately owned units and shared common areas.

children.text: Compare more than the property type. Consider what you can afford, related costs such as utilities, insurance, taxes and other fees, and access to services and amenities.
Hypothetical example:
Sam compares a townhouse and a condo. Sam reviews the total costs and distance to public transportation and grocery stores before deciding which option better meets their needs.

items.question: Do housing costs vary by location?

children.text: Yes. Renting and ownership costs can vary widely among provinces, territories, cities and neighbourhoods.

items.question: What common areas might condo owners share?

children.text: Examples include a lobby, stairs and green spaces.

sources.title: Newcomers: An overview of housing in Canada

sections.question: Which approach can give a buyer a clearer picture of available homes?

options.text: Combine information from several sources with in-person visits when possible
Choose a home without researching its area

sections.explanation: Checking more than one source and visiting communities or homes when possible can provide a fuller view of the options.

children.text: A listing price is only one part of a home search. Buyers can also consider related costs and how close the home is to services and amenities they need.
Hypothetical example:
Sam finds two suitable listings online. Before deciding which one to visit, Sam compares nearby public transportation, grocery stores, utilities, insurance, taxes, and other fees.

items.question: Why should I check more than one source?

children.text: Different sources can help you research communities and find options that meet your needs.

items.question: What location details can I compare?

children.text: Consider access to services and amenities such as public transportation, schools, medical clinics, grocery stores, and cultural communities.

sources.title: Newcomers: An overview of housing in Canada

lessons.title: Lesson 5.1: Key Investment Tools and Accounts in Canada

sections.question: What should you consider before choosing an investment?

options.text: Your risk tolerance, goals, and when you need the money
Only whether the investment pays interest

sections.explanation: An investment should fit your risk tolerance, objectives, and timeline. Possible return is not the only consideration.

children.text: Investment choices can differ in risk and access to money. Consider your goals, timeline, risk tolerance, and any fees before choosing.
Hypothetical example:
Priya expects to need her money soon. Before selecting a GIC, she checks its term and whether an early withdrawal would be limited or penalized.

items.question: Can a TFSA hold investments other than cash?

children.text: Yes. A TFSA can hold cash, bonds, GICs, stocks, and mutual funds.

items.question: Why should I review a mutual fund's fees?

children.text: Fees and the fund’s mix of investments both affect your return.

sources.title: Module 5: Saving and investing

sections.question: Which statement about an expired PR card is correct?

options.text: Your PR status ends automatically when the card expires.
Your PR status does not end just because the card expires.
An expired card automatically makes you a Canadian citizen.

sections.explanation: A PR card proves your status, but its expiry does not automatically end your PR status.

children.text: PR status and a PR card are not the same thing. An expired card does not automatically end PR status. An official decision is required before someone loses PR status for not meeting the residency obligation.
Hypothetical example:
Sam notices that their PR card has expired. Sam does not assume that PR status has ended and checks the official information about status and travel documents.

items.question: Do I lose PR status when my PR card expires?

children.text: No. PR status does not end simply because the card expires.

items.question: What can I use to record trips outside Canada?

children.text: You can use the Government of Canada’s travel journal to track your time in and outside Canada.

sources.title: Understand PR Status

sections.question: What happens when a PR card expires?

options.text: PR status does not end automatically
The person automatically becomes a Canadian citizen

sections.explanation: A PR card proves PR status, but an expired card does not automatically end that status.

children.text: A PR card is proof of permanent resident status. A permanent resident returning to Canada on a commercial vehicle must show a valid PR card and a passport or refugee travel document.
Hypothetical example:
Sam plans to return to Canada by airplane but does not have a valid PR card. Sam checks the official information about applying for a permanent resident travel document before returning.

items.question: Is a permanent resident the same as a Canadian citizen?

children.text: No. A permanent resident has PR status but is not a Canadian citizen.

items.question: Can a COPR or e-COPR be used while waiting for a PR card?

children.text: Yes. It can be used to apply for government services while waiting for the PR card.

sources.title: Understand PR Status - Canada.ca

sections.question: Which item is a main factor used to calculate a credit score?
sections.explanation: Payment history is a main credit-score factor. Language proficiency and education are not listed as credit-score factors.

children.text: Credit scores are based on information in credit reports and other factors. Credit reporting agencies use their own formulas, so the exact calculation is not public.
Hypothetical example:
Priya reviews her credit report and notices that a payment was recorded late. She checks the entry because payment history is one factor used to calculate a credit score.

items.question: Do all organizations calculate credit scores in the same way?

children.text: No. Credit reporting agencies use their own formulas, and lenders may also use their own formulas.

items.question: What information can appear in a credit report?

children.text: It can include account-opening dates, loan applications, balances, payment history, amounts owed, and debts sent to collection agencies.

sources.title: Module 3: Understanding credit

sections.question: Which resume update best tailors it to a job posting?

options.text: Add unrelated details to make the resume longer
Describe relevant achievements using language from the posting
Use the same resume without reviewing the posting

sections.explanation: Job Bank recommends reviewing the job description and including work experience or achievements related to the position.

children.text: A strong work experience section shows what you accomplished, not only the duties you performed. Choose truthful examples that demonstrate skills relevant to the position.
Hypothetical example:
A posting asks for inventory management. Instead of writing “Responsible for inventory,” an applicant describes a real inventory achievement and uses the posting’s term, “inventory management.”

items.question: Should I create a different resume for each application?

children.text: You can adapt each resume to the specific job requirements. Job Bank’s Resume Builder also supports multiple customized resumes.

items.question: What should I check after tailoring my resume?

children.text: Proofread for spelling and grammar, and ask someone else to review it if possible.

sources.title: What is the Resume Builder and how can I use it?
How to write a good resume

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: PR vs. TR vs. Citizen

sections.question: Which status is defined in the source as a foreign national granted permanent resident status?
sections.explanation: The source defines permanent residents as foreign nationals who have been granted permanent resident status.

children.text: Permanent resident status may be granted through economic, family, refugee and protected person, or humanitarian and compassionate and other immigration classes.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is granted permanent resident status through the Family Class. Sam’s immigration class explains the pathway used, while permanent resident describes Sam’s status.

items.question: Are permanent residents and temporary residents the same status?

children.text: No. They are distinct immigration statuses.

items.question: Who is included as a temporary resident in the cited Levels Plan definition?

children.text: International students and temporary workers admitted under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or International Mobility Program.

sources.title: IRCC Minister Transition Binder 2025-05 - The Immigration Levels Plan

sections.question: Which factor can affect a B.C. Basic Autoplan premium?
sections.explanation: ICBC says a customer's location, crash history, vehicle use, and other drivers can affect a Basic insurance premium.

children.text: In B.C., Basic Autoplan premiums reflect the risk and possible cost of a future claim. Relevant factors include where a customer lives, their crash history, how they use the vehicle, and who else may drive it.
Hypothetical example:
Two B.C. customers use their vehicles differently and have different crash histories. Their Basic Autoplan premiums may therefore differ.

items.question: Who provides Basic insurance in British Columbia?

children.text: ICBC is the sole provider of Basic insurance in B.C.

items.question: Are collision and comprehensive coverages part of mandatory Basic Autoplan?

children.text: No. ICBC describes collision and comprehensive as optional coverages available from ICBC and other insurers.

sources.title: What impacts the cost of your insurance?
Basic insurance and Enhanced Care

sections.question: According to TransLink, who may be eligible to apply for the BC Bus Pass Program?

options.text: A low-income senior or a person with a disability

sections.explanation: TransLink says low-income seniors and people with disabilities may be eligible. Eligibility should be checked with the program.

children.text: Transit discounts and fare rules vary by program and rider. Check the local transit authority’s current information before choosing a fare product.
Hypothetical example:
Sam lives in Metro Vancouver and wants a discounted fare. Sam checks TransLink’s fare page to compare Compass options and find the linked BC Bus Pass Program information.

items.question: Does a Compass Card always provide a low-income discount?

children.text: No. TransLink lists different Compass fare products and separate eligibility-based programs. Check which option applies to you.

items.question: Are all TransLink concession fares based on income?

children.text: No. TransLink also lists concession fares for HandyCard holders, seniors, and youth.

sources.title: Pricing and Fare Zones

sections.question: What does a mortgage preapproval guarantee?

options.text: A maximum mortgage amount you may qualify for, but not final approval
The same mortgage terms from every lender

sections.explanation: A preapproval estimates what a lender may offer. Final approval can still depend on factors such as the property and down payment.

children.text: Lenders may use different criteria and offer different rates or conditions. Comparing options and asking how long a rate is guaranteed can help you assess an offer.
Hypothetical example:

A buyer receives a preapproval, then asks the lender how long the rate is guaranteed and whether a lower rate will apply if rates fall. The buyer also considers homes below the maximum amount to leave room for other home-buying costs.

items.question: Can a lender refuse a mortgage after preapproval?

children.text: Yes. Preapproval is not final approval, and the lender may still assess the chosen property and other details.

items.question: What is the difference between a lender and a mortgage broker?

children.text: A lender provides mortgage funds directly. A broker arranges a transaction by finding a lender for the borrower.

sources.title: Getting preapproved for a mortgage

sections.question: What should you do after a lender refuses your mortgage application?

options.text: Ask the lender about other available options
Assume every lender will make the same decision
Treat the earlier preapproval as a mortgage guarantee

sections.explanation: A preapproval does not guarantee a mortgage. If an application is refused, ask the lender about available options, which may include a lower mortgage amount or a larger down payment.

children.text: Each lender has its own guidelines. A refusal from one lender may lead to a discussion about other options, such as a lower mortgage amount.
Hypothetical example:
A buyer’s application is refused. The buyer asks why and learns that the lender may consider a lower mortgage amount. The buyer then reviews that option before deciding what to do.

items.question: Does preapproval guarantee the final mortgage?

children.text: No. The lender still verifies the application and whether the property meets its standards.

items.question: Do all lenders use the same approval rules?

children.text: No. Each lender sets its own lending guidelines and policies.

sources.title: Getting preapproved for a mortgage

sections.question: Who lends mortgage money directly to a borrower?
sections.explanation: A lender provides the money directly. A broker finds a lender and arranges the transaction.

children.text: Brokers may offer access to many lenders, but brokers do not all work with the same lenders. Ask a broker which lenders they work with.
Hypothetical example:
Sam asks a broker for their lender list, then compares the available products with an option offered directly by Sam’s bank.

items.question: Does preapproval guarantee a mortgage?

children.text: No. Final approval can depend on factors such as the property value and the lender’s standards.

items.question: Do all brokers offer the same mortgage products?

children.text: No. Brokers may work with different lenders, so their available products can vary.

sources.title: Getting preapproved for a mortgage

sections.question: Which bullet point best shows a relevant accomplishment?

options.text: Resolved customer requests using the employer's support system

sections.explanation: The correct option uses an action verb, describes a specific contribution, and connects the experience to a relevant tool.

children.text: Start with a clear action verb, identify what you accomplished, and add an accurate result or detail. Review the job description and emphasize experience that matches its requirements.
Hypothetical example:
A posting mentions scheduling and customer service. Instead of “Helped at the front desk,” a candidate writes: “Managed appointment scheduling and responded to customer questions.”

items.question: Should I add a number to every bullet point?

children.text: No. Use firm numbers when they accurately quantify an achievement. Otherwise, give a specific example of your contribution.

items.question: How can I tailor a bullet point?

children.text: Review the job description, then emphasize related accomplishments and use relevant keywords where they truthfully describe your experience.

sources.title: How to write a good resume - Job Bank
Stand out to employers and land your dream job - Job Bank

sections.question: Which action is listed as a requirement for an adult citizenship grant?

options.text: Applying for a provincial birth certificate
Renouncing permanent resident status before applying

sections.explanation: Adult grant requirements include taking the Oath of Citizenship. A provincial or territorial birth certificate can be evidence of citizenship for someone born in Canada.

children.text: The citizenship study guide supports preparation for the knowledge test. It covers topics such as Canadian history, government, symbols and regions.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is preparing for the knowledge test. Sam uses the citizenship study guide to review how Canada’s government works and learn about Canadian symbols.

items.question: Who is responsible for Canadian citizenship?

children.text: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada is responsible for Canadian citizenship, which is governed by the Citizenship Act.

items.question: What forms can a citizenship certificate take?

children.text: A citizenship certificate provided as evidence of citizenship can be paper or electronic.

sources.title: Citizenship Program

sections.question: Why should a newcomer learn the local transit system even if they have used transit elsewhere?

options.text: Transit procedures can differ between cities.
Every Canadian city uses the same procedures.
Transit is available in every rural area.

sections.explanation: Local details can differ, including how riders request a stop, open a bus door, or pay a fare.

children.text: Knowing how to use transit in one place does not guarantee that every local procedure will be familiar. Learning how to board, request a stop, exit, pay, and ask for help can make travel easier.
Hypothetical example:
Sam moves to Metro Vancouver and takes a practice trip before commuting. Sam learns how to signal for a stop and open the bus door, then feels better prepared for the regular journey.

items.question: What local transit details may be unfamiliar?

children.text: Stop signals, bus doors, payment methods, and ways to get help may differ.

items.question: How can travel training help?

children.text: It can provide hands-on practice with buses and stations, including boarding, exiting, finding information, and asking for help.

sources.title: Travel-training workshops aim to set new riders up for success
TransLink Podcast: How we're helping newcomers learn to use the transit system

sections.question: What can a rider do before leaving a Metro Vancouver bus at their stop?

options.text: Signal the stop and follow the instructions for opening the rear door
Wait for the bus to return to its starting point
Use a Compass Vending Machine on the bus

sections.explanation: Metro Vancouver buses have features for signalling a stop. Riders may also need to follow instructions to open the rear door.

children.text: Transit routines differ between cities. Learning how to signal a stop, open bus doors, use fare equipment, and ask for help can make travel easier.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is taking a Metro Vancouver bus for the first time. Before the trip, Sam learns how to signal the stop and checks how the rear door opens. This helps Sam leave at the planned stop.

items.question: What practical skills can a new rider learn?

children.text: They can learn how to board and leave a bus, signal a stop, use fare equipment, and find help or information.

items.question: Where can riders seek help at a SkyTrain station?

children.text: They can ask a SkyTrain or Canada Line attendant. Telephones on SkyTrain platforms can also be used for assistance.

sources.title: Travel-training workshops aim to set new riders up for success
TransLink Podcast: How we're helping newcomers learn to use the transit system

sections.question: Why should you learn how your local transit system works?

options.text: Transit procedures can differ between cities.
Every Canadian city uses the same procedures.
Bus doors always open in the same way.

sections.explanation: Transit systems can have different ways to signal a stop, open a bus door, pay, or get help.

children.text: Knowing a route is only part of using transit. Riders may also need to learn local procedures, such as how to request a stop, leave a bus, pay, or ask for assistance.
Hypothetical example:
Sam plans a Metro Vancouver trip. Before travelling, Sam checks how to signal a bus stop and use the rear door, then identifies where to ask for help at the SkyTrain station.

items.question: What local transit details should I check?

children.text: Check how to board, pay, request your stop, exit, transfer, and get assistance.

items.question: Can hands-on instruction help a new rider?

children.text: Yes. TransLink’s travel training demonstrates bus features, getting on and off, buying a Compass Card, and finding help.

sources.title: Travel-training workshops aim to set new riders up for success
TransLink Podcast: How we're helping newcomers learn to use the transit system

sections.question: Which support was part of the Fredericton youth sports program?
sections.explanation: The local program offered equipment loans and transportation assistance to reduce barriers. This does not mean the same support is available in every community.

children.text: Recreation support may involve more than reduced access fees. A local program may also connect participants with equipment, transportation, coaching, or mentors. Available support depends on the community and program.
Hypothetical example:
Sam wants to join a local sport but needs equipment. Sam checks the local program details and asks whether equipment loans are available before registering.

items.question: Can I expect every community to offer the same support?

children.text: No. Local programs can take different forms, so check what is offered in your community.

items.question: Where can an eligible newcomer look for settlement help?

children.text: IRCC has a service finder that can search by postal code, city, province, or territory. Call or email before visiting to confirm the service you want is available.

sources.title: Newcomer Youth Participation in Sports (NYPS)
Find free newcomer services near you

sections.question: What should you do if you want to live in SFU residence?
sections.explanation: Residence spaces are limited, so SFU recommends applying as early as possible.

children.text: Because residence space is limited, it is useful to apply early and also learn about off-campus options.
Hypothetical example:
Sam applies for residence early. Sam also reviews SFU’s off-campus housing resources in case a residence room is unavailable.

items.question: What kinds of off-campus homes are available in Metro Vancouver?

children.text: Options include apartments, houses, and townhouses.

items.question: Where can I find help with an off-campus housing search?

children.text: SFU’s Off-Campus Housing page provides listing services, rental-scam information, and tenancy resources.

sources.title: Housing Options
Off-Campus Housing

sections.question: Which request may be a warning sign of a rental scam?

options.text: A request for a deposit before you view the unit
An offer to arrange an in-person viewing
A request for references before committing to a tenant

sections.explanation: SFU lists a request for a deposit before viewing as a possible warning sign. It also suggests comparing the rent with similar units and checking whether an in-person viewing is available.

children.text: Before committing to a rental, compare its price with similar local units and confirm that the person advertising it will arrange a viewing.
Hypothetical example:
Sam finds an unusually inexpensive apartment. The advertiser asks for a deposit but refuses a viewing. Sam does not send money and continues checking other listings.

items.question: Does SFU inspect listings on Places4Students?

children.text: No. SFU says it does not screen, inspect, warrant, or approve the landlords or accommodations listed there.

items.question: What kinds of off-campus homes may be available in Metro Vancouver?

children.text: Options may include apartments, houses, and townhouses.

sources.title: Housing Options
Off-Campus Housing

sections.question: If you plan to transfer from a college to a university in B.C., what should you check before starting?

options.text: Which courses the university will recognize for credit
Whether tuition is the same at every institution

sections.explanation: The receiving institution checks completed courses and decides which ones receive credit. Not all courses are recognized by every institution.

children.text: A transfer pathway can connect study at one institution with a program at another. Students should confirm how completed courses may count toward the intended credential.
Hypothetical example:
Lina wants to begin at a public college and later finish a degree at a university. Before registering, she checks which college courses the university recognizes for transfer credit.

items.question: What kinds of post-secondary study are available in B.C.?

children.text: Options include academic programs, career training, skilled-trades training, English learning, and skills upgrading.

items.question: Can post-secondary study be completed online?

children.text: Many B.C. colleges and universities offer distributed or distance-learning programs. Available options depend on the institution.

sources.title: WelcomeBC - Start Your New life in B.C.
Start your life in BC - WelcomeBC

sections.question: Which option can let a student begin at one institution and later continue at a university?
sections.explanation: A university transfer program can support moving from a college or institute to a university. The receiving institution checks which completed courses qualify for credit.

children.text: The type of institution is only one part of a decision. A student can also compare programs, prerequisites, credentials, delivery methods, and whether courses may transfer.
Hypothetical example:

Sam wants career-focused technical training and may later continue studying. Sam compares institute programs and checks in advance whether completed courses could receive credit at another institution.

items.question: Can post-secondary study be completed from a distance?

children.text: Yes. Many B.C. colleges and universities offer distributed or distance learning programs.

items.question: Will every completed course transfer to another institution?

children.text: No. The receiving institution decides which courses receive credit, so students should check transfer information before starting.

sources.title: WelcomeBC - Start Your New life in B.C.
Start your life in BC - WelcomeBC

sections.question: Which resource can help a student explore programs and apply in British Columbia?
sections.explanation: EducationPlannerBC helps people explore education and careers, find programs, and apply for programs.

children.text: Admission requirements can differ by program. Check the prerequisites and required courses for the specific program before applying.
Hypothetical example:
Sam finds a career-training program through EducationPlannerBC. Before applying, Sam reads the program page to confirm the prerequisites and required courses.

items.question: Where can I find a list of post-secondary institutions in British Columbia?

children.text: The WelcomeBC resources directory links to a list of post-secondary institutions in B.C.

items.question: What should I check before choosing a career-training program?

children.text: Check the program’s prerequisites and the courses needed to complete it.

sources.title: WelcomeBC - Start Your New life in B.C.
Start your life in BC - WelcomeBC

sections.question: Which cost should a student include when planning to study in a different city?
sections.explanation: A complete plan includes tuition and other fees, books and materials, housing, living costs, and transportation.

children.text: Compare the full cost of each study option, not only tuition. Check school fees, books, materials, housing, living costs, and transportation. Ask the school’s financial aid office about available support.
Hypothetical example:
Sam compares two B.C. programs. Sam lists each school’s tuition and other fees, then adds expected books, housing, living costs, and transportation before choosing a program.

items.question: Where can I ask about financial help?

children.text: Contact the financial aid office at the school you plan to attend.

items.question: Is financial aid available at every private institution?

children.text: No. It is available at some private institutions, so check whether the institution qualifies for student aid funding.

Start your life in BC - WelcomeBC

sections.question: Which action can help a student build community?
sections.explanation: Joining clubs can help students meet people and build networks.

children.text: Different campus services address different needs. Identifying the need first can help a student choose an appropriate service.
Hypothetical example:
A student wants feedback on an essay. They contact the writing centre rather than career services.

items.question: Where can a student seek help with writing?

children.text: They can ask whether their institution has a writing centre or tutoring service.

items.question: What can help a student meet people outside class?

children.text: Joining clubs, volunteering, and attending events can create opportunities to connect with others.

sources.title: WelcomeBC - Start your life in B.C.

sections.question: Which option is a form of further education after a bachelor's degree?
sections.explanation: A master's degree is a graduate degree that can be pursued after earning a bachelor's degree.

children.text: Further study can build knowledge or career skills. In B.C., post-secondary options include graduate degrees, certificates, and other credentials.
Hypothetical example:
After completing a bachelor’s degree, Sam compares a master’s program with a professional certificate to decide which better fits their goals.

items.question: What graduate degrees can follow a bachelor's degree?

children.text: A student may continue to a master’s or doctorate degree.

items.question: Where can I find information about B.C. post-secondary institutions?

children.text: WelcomeBC provides information about post-secondary education and a resource directory with a list of institutions.

sections.question: Which option can help someone connect with people in their community?

options.text: Waiting for others to make every connection

sections.explanation: Social clubs are one way to connect with people in your community.

children.text: Community activities can create opportunities to meet people. Options may include volunteering, community centres, sports teams, social clubs, settlement organizations, and places of worship.
Hypothetical example:
A student who enjoys community service visits a volunteering group, speaks with its members, and decides whether the group feels right for them.

items.question: What if joining a new group feels stressful?

children.text: Adjusting and making new friends can be difficult. You can ask your school or a local settlement service provider about available support.

items.question: Are clubs the only way to meet people?

children.text: No. Other options include volunteering, community centres, sports teams, settlement organizations, and places of worship.

Welcoming women in Canada

sections.question: Which item on a credit report may be a sign of identity theft?

options.text: An account you did not open
A payment correctly marked as on time

sections.explanation: An unfamiliar account may mean someone applied for credit in your name. Examine it to determine whether it involves fraud or identity theft.

children.text: A fraud alert tells lenders that you may be a victim of fraud. Before approving a credit application, they need to contact you and confirm your identity.
Hypothetical example:
Sam finds an unfamiliar account on a credit report. Sam contacts the affected lender and asks both Equifax and TransUnion to place a fraud alert on the report.

items.question: Why should I get my credit report from both credit bureaus?

children.text: Reviewing reports from both Equifax and TransUnion may help you detect errors or fraud sooner.

items.question: What information should I check besides unfamiliar accounts?

children.text: Check personal details, credit cards, loans, and payment history for mistakes.

sources.title: Checking your credit report for errors and fraud

sections.question: Which income must a Canadian resident gig worker report for tax purposes?

options.text: Only income earned through Canadian platforms

sections.explanation: The CRA says resident gig workers must report all self-employment income, including income from business done outside Canada.

children.text: Employment income includes wages or salary from an employer. Money earned from services carried on for profit can be business income. Gig workers should track their income and expenses.
Hypothetical example:
Sam earns a salary and also completes freelance design work through an online platform. Sam keeps the freelance transaction records and reports the self-employment income separately from the salary.

items.question: What is gig work?

children.text: It generally means short-term contracts, freelance work, or temporary work arranged through an online platform or mobile application.

items.question: What records should gig workers keep?

children.text: They should track income, expenses, and transactions, including sales to buyers in Canada and other countries.

sources.title: Small businesses and self-employed income
Gig economy - Taxes and the platform economy

lessons.title: Getting a Driver’s Licence in Canada

sections.question: In British Columbia, which licence follows the learner’s L stage?
sections.explanation: British Columbia’s graduated licensing program moves from the L learner’s licence to the N novice licence and then to a full Class 5 licence.

children.text: Licence stages and exchange rules depend on the province. A person should use information for the province where they will be licensed.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is moving from another country to British Columbia. Sam checks ICBC’s rules to learn whether the existing licence can be exchanged and what proof of driving experience may be needed.

items.question: Who issues driver’s licences to British Columbia residents?

children.text: ICBC issues driver’s licences to British Columbia residents.

items.question: What may affect whether a foreign licence can be exchanged?

children.text: It depends on the province and whether it has an exchange agreement with the licence’s place of origin.

Driver licensing & ID

sections.question: What happens after an online questionnaire for a work permit application?

options.text: You receive a personalized document checklist
You automatically receive a work permit
You no longer need to submit documents

sections.explanation: The questionnaire produces a personalized checklist showing the documents required for the application.

children.text: Work permit applications are made online in almost all cases. An applicant uses an IRCC secure account to upload forms and documents and submit a complete application.
Hypothetical example:
Sam answers the online questionnaire, reviews the personalized document checklist, creates electronic copies of the requested documents, and uploads them through the secure account.

items.question: What equipment may be needed to upload documents online?

children.text: A scanner or camera can create electronic copies of the documents.

items.question: Why should an applicant review the document checklist carefully?

children.text: A work permit application may be refused if required documents or information are missing.

sources.title: Work permit: Apply inside Canada – Step-by-step instructions & fees
Application to work in Canada - work permits including open work permits

sections.question: Which program is employer-driven and supports skilled foreign workers and international graduates from an Atlantic Canadian institution?
sections.explanation: The Atlantic Immigration Program is employer-driven. The other two programs are managed through Express Entry.

children.text: Express Entry manages three federal programs and part of the Provincial Nominee Program. Regional pathways may instead focus on the needs of a province, Atlantic employers, or participating rural communities.
Hypothetical example:
Sam has eligible Canadian skilled work experience. Sam compares the Canadian Experience Class requirements with regional pathways before choosing which option to explore.

items.question: Is a job offer required for every Express Entry program?

children.text: No. It is not required for the Canadian Experience Class or Federal Skilled Worker Program. Different rules apply to the Federal Skilled Trades Program.

items.question: What happens to an Express Entry candidate who receives a provincial nomination?

children.text: The candidate receives extra points, which can help them receive an invitation to apply.

Economic Immigration

sections.question: What useful step can help you learn from an interview?

options.text: Reflect on what worked and what you would do differently
Send the same generic message to every interviewer
Ask about salary in the thank-you note

sections.explanation: Reviewing what went well and what did not can help you prepare for future interviews.

children.text: After sending your thank-you note, reflect on the interview. Identify what worked, what did not, and what you might say or do differently next time.
Hypothetical example:
Sam remembers giving a clear answer about training but struggling to explain a work experience. Sam plans to rehearse that answer before the next interview.

items.question: What should I do if an employer misses an agreed call time?

children.text: Make a polite follow-up call.

items.question: What can I ask if I did not get the job?

children.text: You can politely ask what would have made you a better candidate.

sources.title: Preparing for an interview

sections.question: When does a law become enforceable?
sections.explanation: A law becomes enforceable once it comes into force.

children.text: Regulations support laws, carry out their purposes, and are enforceable by law. They are made by people or bodies that received authority through an Act.
Hypothetical example:
A person checks the local waste instructions before choosing a bin because disposal rules may be specific to the community.

items.question: Why do laws matter in everyday life?

children.text: They govern many everyday activities and help support a safe, peaceful, and orderly society.

items.question: Are regulations enforceable?

children.text: Yes. Regulations support laws and are enforceable by law.

sources.title: How new laws and regulations are created

sections.question: What is a useful first step when reviewing transportation spending?

options.text: Track what you spend and where you spend it
Choose a fare without checking local rules

sections.explanation: Tracking expenses gives you a clear picture of your spending and can help you identify possible savings.

children.text: Compare your travel pattern with local fare choices, and review statements for errors or unfamiliar charges. Planning ahead can reveal ways to reduce spending.
Hypothetical example:
Sam records each transit payment, checks the local transit rules, and compares the available fare choices before deciding which one fits their usual travel.

items.question: Why should I track transportation spending?

children.text: It helps you understand where your money goes and identify areas where you may be able to cut back.

items.question: What should I do if I see an unfamiliar charge?

children.text: Check your statement carefully and contact the service provider to ask about the charge.

sources.title: Module 2: How do I live within my means?

sections.question: What kind of tax credit is the tuition tax credit?

options.text: A tuition refund from the school

sections.explanation: The tuition tax credit is non-refundable. It can reduce income tax payable based on eligible tuition fees.

children.text: The amount shown on an official tax form or receipt identifies eligible tuition fees for the calendar year. Some fees may not qualify, including certain amounts paid or reimbursed through an employer or government program.
Hypothetical example:

A student sees tuition on a school receipt and an employer reimbursement. Before claiming an amount, the student checks the official tax form and whether the reimbursement is excluded under the rules.

items.question: Does every fee charged by a school qualify?

children.text: No. Eligibility depends on the type of fee and the applicable rules. The official tax form or receipt indicates eligible tuition fees.

items.question: Can unused tuition credits be transferred instead of carried forward?

children.text: They may be transferred to certain family members, subject to requirements and limits.

sections.question: Which topic can be part of retirement planning?

options.text: A guaranteed benefit amount for every retiree

sections.explanation: Canada's retirement information identifies when to start pensions as one topic to consider. Nationality varies, and the source does not guarantee one benefit amount for everyone.

children.text: Retirement planning can include considering when to start pensions, whether to work while receiving public pensions, how to live with limited income, and options for living abroad.
Hypothetical example:
A retired visitor reviews their travel documents and insurance, then uses Canada’s retirement-planning tools to explore income options before travelling.

items.question: What tools can help someone estimate retirement income?

children.text: Canada.ca lists the Canada Retirement Income Calculator and the Old Age Security Benefits Estimator.

children.text: Yes. Canada’s retirement guidance includes options for living abroad among the topics to consider.

sections.question: Which number connects callers to a B.C. crisis line and does not require an area code?
sections.explanation: The Mental Health and Information Support Line is reached at 310-6789 without an area code. It provides emotional support and information about appropriate B.C. mental health referrals.

children.text: Different services meet different needs. A person can use a community directory or navigator to find nearby mental health support, while a crisis line provides immediate emotional support and referral information.
Hypothetical example:
Sam wants local counselling but does not know what is available. Sam calls HealthLink BC at 8-1-1 and asks a health service navigator for help finding care in the community.

items.question: What should I do in a life-threatening emergency?

children.text: Call 9-1-1 or go to the nearest hospital emergency room.

sections.question: In British Columbia, which service can help someone find care in their community?
sections.explanation: HealthLink BC 8-1-1 has health service navigators who can help people find care in their community.

children.text: In British Columbia, a health service navigator can help someone locate health services and facilities in their area.

Sam wants local mental health support but does not know where to begin. Sam contacts HealthLink BC 8-1-1 and asks a navigator about care nearby.

items.question: Can HealthLink BC help me find care in my community?

children.text: Yes. In B.C., an 8-1-1 health service navigator can help you find community care.

children.text: Help Starts Here provides searchable service listings and a map for supports across B.C.

sections.question: Who can help a newcomer youth find information about scholarships and grants?
sections.explanation: Local settlement service providers may help newcomer youth access scholarships and grants.

children.text: Eligibility differs by program. If you are unsure, ask the program to confirm, ask your school, or contact a local settlement service provider.
Hypothetical example:
Sam finds an award but does not know whether their immigration status qualifies. Sam asks the award provider to confirm and contacts a settlement service provider for help.

items.question: What should I do if I am unsure whether I qualify?

children.text: Ask the program to confirm. You can also ask your school or a local settlement service provider.

items.question: Are scholarships available at different study levels?

children.text: Yes. Canada.ca lists scholarships, awards, and bursaries for undergraduate, graduate, doctoral, and post-doctoral study.

sections.question: Which action helps prevent important mail or cards from being missed?

options.text: Update your address with the relevant agencies

sections.explanation: Keeping your address current with IRCC, CRA, and your province helps important mail and cards reach you.

children.text: A simple setup plan can help you track applications, address updates, and important records.

Sam applies for a SIN and the provincial health plan, then stores related letters with tax records. After moving, Sam updates the relevant agencies.

items.question: Why should I keep tax, health, and SIN documents?

children.text: They provide a record of important notices, forms, and correspondence.

items.question: Can people in British Columbia view health information online?

children.text: Yes. Health Gateway provides B.C. patients with secure online access to many health records, although it does not contain every record.

sections.question: What happens to permanent resident status when a PR card expires?

options.text: The person remains a permanent resident
The person must apply for permanent residence again

sections.explanation: An expired PR card does not end permanent resident status. However, a valid PR card or PRTD may be needed to return to Canada by commercial transportation.

children.text: A permanent resident outside Canada without a valid PR card needs a PRTD when returning by airplane, boat, train or bus.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is outside Canada and discovers that their PR card has expired. Sam plans to return by bus, so they apply for a PRTD before travelling.

items.question: Is a valid PR card needed when transiting through a Canadian airport?

children.text: Yes. A permanent resident needs a valid PR card when transiting through a Canadian airport.

items.question: What can happen if a PRTD application is missing information or documents?

children.text: The application will be returned.

sections.question: What is one purpose of the Advisory Council on Rights, Equality and Inclusion?

options.text: To advise the federal minister on rights, equality and inclusion
To manage every workplace and school

sections.explanation: The Council provides advice to the minister and supports efforts to protect rights, strengthen inclusion and combat racism and hate.

children.text: Inclusion can involve listening to communities and coordinating organizations that work to protect rights and address racism and hate.

A community group invites people with different experiences to discuss barriers to belonging. It uses their feedback to improve an inclusion initiative.

items.question: Who contributes to the federal Advisory Council's work?

children.text: Experts and community leaders contribute advice, including people from civil society, academia, youth leadership and Indigenous communities.

items.question: What does social inclusion seek to strengthen?

children.text: The source connects social inclusion with trust, belonging and understanding among communities.

sections.question: When does confirming that you are in Canada mean you have become a permanent resident?

options.text: As soon as you make the declaration
When IRCC uploads your e-COPR to the portal
Only when your PR card arrives

sections.explanation: Declaring that you are in Canada does not make you a permanent resident. Your e-COPR confirms your permanent resident status.

children.text: Use the account identified by IRCC. If you applied through the Permanent Residence Portal, use that account. Otherwise, IRCC creates an account and sends sign-in details.
Hypothetical example:
Sam applied through the Permanent Residence Portal. After receiving the confirmation message, Sam signs in to the same account rather than creating a new one.

items.question: What should I do if information on my e-COPR is incorrect?

children.text: Request an amendment to the information in the COPR.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1:  Key Terms & Common Account Types

sections.question: Which account type can include a chequing or savings account?
sections.explanation: CRA guidance lists commercial, chequing, savings, time, and thrift accounts as types of depository accounts.

children.text: A financial account is an account maintained by a financial institution. Depository accounts include chequing and savings accounts.
Hypothetical example:
Sam wants one account for regular purchases and another for money not needed for daily spending. Sam compares a chequing account with a savings account based on those different purposes.

items.question: Is a chequing account a depository account?

children.text: Yes. CRA guidance includes chequing accounts in its definition of depository accounts.

items.question: Can a Canadian financial institution ask about tax residence?

children.text: Yes. It may ask an account holder to certify or clarify tax residence or provide supporting documents for tax reporting.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.2: Resources for Credit Cards in Canada

sections.question: Which resource can compare credit card interest rates, annual fees, rewards, and other features?
sections.explanation: The Credit Card Comparison Tool compares interest rates, annual fees, rewards, and other card features.

children.text: A useful comparison considers interest rates, annual fees, rewards, and other features. These details can help distinguish cards that may otherwise seem similar.
Hypothetical example:
Priya finds two credit cards with different fees and rewards. She uses the government comparison tool to review both cards before deciding which better matches her needs.

items.question: Where can I learn how credit card interest, fees, and penalties work?

children.text: Canada.ca provides information about how credit cards work, including transactions, interest, fees, and penalties.

items.question: Is there a government tool for estimating how long repayment may take?

children.text: Yes. The Credit Card Payment Calculator estimates how long repayment may take and lets you explore faster repayment options.

sources.title: Credit cards

lessons.title: Lesson 9.2: Travel Documents: PR Card vs PRTD

sections.question: Which document can a permanent resident outside Canada use to board a commercial carrier to Canada if they do not have a valid PR card?
sections.explanation: A PRTD is used in place of a valid PR card for travel to Canada by a commercial carrier. A Record of Landing or Confirmation of Permanent Residence is not valid for this purpose.

children.text: A PRTD is a temporary travel document, not a PR status document. An officer assesses the application, including the applicant’s PR status and residency obligation.
Hypothetical example:
Sam is a permanent resident outside Canada whose PR card has expired. Sam plans to return on a commercial bus, so Sam applies for a PRTD and provides supporting documents for assessment.

items.question: Can I apply for a PR card while outside Canada?

children.text: No. You can apply for a PR card after returning to Canada.

items.question: Does a PRTD itself prove permanent resident status?

children.text: No. It is an immigration document issued in place of a PR card for travel, not a status document.
